strengths: The core idea (GQR) is well-motivated and technically clean: using a lightweight text retriever's score distribution as soft guidance to refine a vision-centric retriever's query embedding via KL minimization on a candidate pool, rather than crude rank/score fusion, is a sensible middle ground between coarse hybrid fusion and infeasible representation-level fusion.

Extensive empirical evaluation: 9 primary/complementary retriever pairs, 8 hybrid baselines (both untuned and tuned variants), two benchmarks (ViDoRe 1 and 2), latency and memory measurements, and comparisons against cross-encoder rerankers at multiple candidate sizes.

Strong practical results: GQR consistently outperforms other hybrid fusion baselines and yields meaningful NDCG@5 gains over base ColPali-style retrievers on ViDoRe 2, while achieving large efficiency gains (up to 14x faster, 54x less memory) relative to the strongest large multi-vector model, effectively shifting the Pareto frontier.

Thorough ablations in Section 4.2 (extra search stage, candidate pool policy, choice of divergence objective, primary/complementary role swapping) that probe the robustness and design choices of the method, lending credibility to the approach.

Good related work coverage situating the method against ranking-level and score-level hybrid retrieval fusion techniques and prior test-time query refinement work using cross-encoders, clearly articulating the novelty of replacing a cross-encoder with a bi-encoder guidance signal.

Method is architecture-agnostic (applicable to single- and multi-vector retrievers) and the paper provides reasonably detailed implementation/hyperparameter information (Appendix D) supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Gains on ViDoRe 2 are relatively modest in absolute terms (roughly +1 to +3 NDCG@5 points on average) and on ViDoRe 1 the method is essentially neutral (near 0% change), raising questions about the generality/significance of the improvement, especially given the added complexity and inference-time cost of iterative optimization.

The method requires per-subset/per-dataset hyperparameter tuning (learning rate, T) on a held-out in-domain development set, which the authors acknowledge as a limitation; this undermines claims of a practical, deployable, zero-shot-ready solution and makes the reported gains less clearly attributable to the guidance mechanism versus tuning effort (the tuned score-aggregation baselines already close much of the gap to GQR).

The comparison to tuned score-aggregation baselines shows a relatively small margin (avg 3.9% vs 3.4%/2.6% for tuned min-max/softmax score aggregation), suggesting the added algorithmic complexity of GQR (iterative gradient-based optimization per query) may not be justified by the incremental gain over simpler tuned alternatives, especially considering the extra latency overhead GQR introduces relative to those baselines (which the paper does not clearly quantify against GQR's latency).

No statistical significance testing or variance/confidence intervals are reported for the NDCG@5 deltas, despite many reported improvements being small (e.g., +0.3, +1.2) and some negative deltas appearing within the same model in different subsets, making it hard to assess whether observed differences are robust versus noise across the relatively small number of benchmark subsets.

The theoretical justification for the specific consensus/KL formulation is thin - the paper is explicitly empirical and does not analyze convergence properties, sensitivity to T/learning rate broadly, or why minimizing KL(p_avg || p1) rather than alternative distances yields the reported benefits beyond an ablation showing 'they perform similarly' (Table 16), which somewhat undercuts the specific design choice as being non-critical/arbitrary.

Evaluation is limited to only two benchmark families (ViDoRe 1 and 2) which are both visual document retrieval specific; it's unclear how well GQR would generalize to other multimodal or even purely textual/mixed retrieval settings, limiting the demonstrated scope of the contribution's significance.

The paper does not clearly report or compare GQR's latency against the tuned score-aggregation baselines (only against base models and rerankers), leaving open whether GQR's added optimization overhead is justified relative to the closest-performing simpler baselines.

Only one reranker (MonoQwen2-VL) is used for comparison, and the reranker comparison uses GQR with a fixed configuration (K=10, Linq-Embed) rather than exploring whether other GQR configurations would fare better/worse, limiting the robustness of the reranker comparison conclusions.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated method (GQR) that occupies a useful middle ground between coarse-grained rank/score fusion and full representation-level fusion, addressing a genuine problem (cost of state-of-the-art ColPali-style multi-vector retrievers).

Extensive empirical evaluation across three benchmarks (ViDoRe 1, 2, 3), 9 primary/complementary model pairs, and both tuned and zero-shot settings, which lends good support to the generality of the method.

Strong and clearly quantified efficiency results: GQR-augmented lightweight models match or exceed a much larger SOTA model (Llama-Nemo) while being up to 14x faster and 54x more memory efficient, with a clear Pareto-frontier analysis for latency, memory, and quality.

Good set of ablations: hyperparameter sweep over learning rate/steps, alternative loss functions (JS, KL-target), candidate pool policy, extra index search, and swapping primary/complementary roles, which increase confidence in the robustness of the design choices.
Comparison to a cross-encoder-style multimodal reranker (MonoQwen2-VL) shows GQR remains on the Pareto front, strengthening the practical relevance claim.
Clear method exposition (algorithm, figures) and reasonable positioning relative to related work on hybrid search and test-time query refinement.
Per-query qualitative analysis (rank dynamics heatmaps) helps illustrate how GQR differs mechanistically from simple score averaging.
weaknesses: Absolute performance gains are often modest (1-4 NDCG@5 points), and the margin over the best-tuned simple baseline (Score Aggregation Min-Max, Tuned) is fairly small on ViDoRe 2 (62.3 vs 62.1), raising the question of whether the added complexity/latency of iterative gradient-based optimization is clearly justified over simpler tuned score fusion.

GQR and the tuned hybrid baselines rely on per-subset development-set hyperparameter tuning, which may not reflect realistic single-configuration production deployment; the zero-shot ViDoRe 3 experiments partially address this but use hyperparameters selected via a single held-out plot rather than a principled selection procedure.

The core technical idea (test-time query refinement via pseudo-relevance feedback/KL minimization) is adapted fairly directly from prior text-only work (Sung et al. 2023; Yu et al. 2021; Gangi Reddy et al. 2025), with the main novelty being its application to a lightweight bi-encoder as guidance and cross-modal (text-vision) setting rather than a fundamentally new formulation.
The paper only explores the two-retriever (M=2) case despite claiming the formulation generalizes to M retrievers; no experiments validate this claimed generality.
The ablation on loss functions (KL vs JS vs KL-target) shows they perform similarly, which somewhat undercuts the specific motivation given for the chosen KL(pavg||p1) objective.

Latency/memory numbers are reported from a single hardware setup (one A100 GPU), and the sequential latency breakdown likely overstates real-world costs if retrievers were parallelized, complicating direct comparison to the highlighted 14x/54x figures.

Limited discussion of failure cases beyond aggregate subset deltas; some subsets and configurations show performance decreases (e.g., Colnomic + Qwen3 on Biomed Lectures) without deeper analysis of when/why GQR can hurt performance.
